output.title: Test assumptions by narrowing one workflow
output.body:
If you want to design against untested assumptions, start by narrowing the decision. Don’t ask, “Can AI do this?” Ask, “Which one recurring workflow is repetitive, measurable, already in digital tools, and written in English-language documents?”

That is the first filter. A demo can make a task look easier than it is, because the hard parts usually sit around the task: data quality, approval steps, handover work, and whether the outcome is actually measurable. If those parts are vague, the build is still vague.

For a small business owner, the practical step is to write down one workflow and check four things: how often it happens, what outcome you can observe, whether it lives in digital tools and English-language documents, and where human approval must stay in place. Money movement and other high-risk decisions stay human. That is not a feature gap; it is the control.

Bareni works inside the customer’s environment, and finished code is handed over while database, automation-tool, and API accounts are in the customer’s name from the start. That is policy and no-lock-in positioning, not an absolute legal warranty.

If the workflow cannot be named clearly, it is probably not ready for automation yet.
